# The Work That Doesn't Show

For most of the twentieth century, the British had a phrase for a task that never ends: "like painting the Forth Bridge." The Forth Bridge is a great red cantilevered railway bridge in Scotland, opened in 1890, and the story went that it was so large, and the Scottish weather so hard on it, that a crew of painters worked continuously along its length. By the time they reached the far end, the near end needed painting again. So they turned around and started over, forever.

The story wasn't quite true. The painting was more patchwork than a single endless sweep. But it was true enough to become an idiom, and I've always liked that the idiom exists. It's one of the few places in ordinary speech where we acknowledge a basic fact about the world: most of what keeps things standing is not building but upkeep. In 2011 the bridge was finally given a new coating expected to last decades, and the endless painting stopped. Newspapers ran stories about it with a note of loss, as if something had gone out of the world. I think something had. A living emblem of maintenance had been retired.

I want to write about maintenance, because I think it is one of the most important and least celebrated activities humans engage in, and because the more I think about it, the more it seems to sit underneath almost everything else.

---

Our stories about progress are almost entirely stories about invention. We remember who built the first steam engine, who discovered penicillin, who wrote the first line of code for some famous program. We have prizes for breakthroughs, for firsts, for originality. We don't have a Nobel Prize for keeping the water treatment plant running without incident for thirty-one years, though that plant has saved more lives than most novels have changed.

It isn't hard to see why. Invention makes a good story. There's a before and an after, a moment of change, a protagonist. Maintenance has no plot. Its success looks exactly like nothing happening. When the bridge doesn't collapse, when the server doesn't go down, when the child doesn't get cholera, there's no event to report. Maintenance is the art of producing non-events. It shows up in the news only when it fails: the levee breaks, the pipes leach lead, the power grid freezes. Then everyone suddenly remembers that someone was supposed to be taking care of it.

In 1969 the artist Mierle Laderman Ukeles wrote a document she called the "Manifesto for Maintenance Art 1969!" She had recently become a mother, and she found herself caught between two identities that her culture treated as incompatible. There was the artist, who was supposed to make new things, be avant-garde, break with the past. And there was the mother, whose days were consumed with washing, feeding, cleaning, changing, and then doing all of it again. The first kind of work was called creation. The second was barely called work at all.

Her manifesto divided the world into two systems: "Development," meaning pure individual creation, the new, change, progress, and "Maintenance," meaning keeping the dust off the pure individual creation, preserving the new, sustaining the change, protecting progress. And then she asked, in effect: why is only the first one art?

She went on to do something remarkable. She became an unsalaried artist-in-residence at the New York City Department of Sanitation, a post she has held for decades. For one of her projects, she spent nearly a year visiting every sanitation district in the city, shaking hands with more than eight thousand sanitation workers, and saying to each of them: "Thank you for keeping New York City alive."

I find that sentence moving every time I read it. It's so simple. It's also accurate in a way that feels almost shocking once you think about it. A city without garbage collection doesn't just become unpleasant. Within weeks it becomes a place where disease spreads. The people who haul trash are, in the most literal sense, keeping the city alive, and until Ukeles showed up, very few people had ever said so to their faces.

---

There's a very old puzzle, the Ship of Theseus. The Athenians preserved the ship of their legendary hero, and as its planks rotted they replaced them one by one with new timber. Eventually, the story goes, no original plank remained. Was it still the same ship?

Philosophers usually treat this as a puzzle about identity, and it's a good one. But I've come to think it's also, quietly, a story about maintenance, and that framed that way it looks less like a paradox and more like a description of how nearly everything that lasts actually lasts.

Consider the Ise Grand Shrine in Japan. For roughly thirteen hundred years, with some interruptions, its main sanctuaries have been completely torn down and rebuilt every twenty years on an adjacent plot, using fresh cypress and traditional techniques. The most recent rebuilding was in 2013. The next is scheduled for 2033. The shrine is, in one sense, never more than twenty years old. In another sense it is among the oldest continuous things in Japan.

What is actually being preserved at Ise isn't wood. It's knowledge. A twenty-year cycle is, not coincidentally, about the length of a working generation. The carpenters who rebuild the shrine as young apprentices will be the master craftsmen at the next rebuilding, and they will teach the apprentices who will lead the one after that. The shrine is a machine for keeping a skill alive. The building is almost a byproduct.

Or consider the Q'eswachaka bridge in the Andes of Peru, a suspension bridge woven from grass rope that spans a gorge over the Apurímac River. It's a remnant of the Inca road system, and every year the surrounding communities gather, twist new cords from grass, braid them into thick cables, and build the bridge anew, letting the old one fall into the river below. Grass rots quickly. A grass bridge left alone would last only a few seasons. A grass bridge maintained by a community has lasted for centuries.

There's something here that runs against our instincts. We tend to think that the way to make something last is to make it out of durable material: stone, steel, titanium. And sometimes that works. But the most durable things humans have made are often not the hardest. They're the ones embedded in a practice of care. A stone monument that no one tends will crack and topple and get carted off for building material. A grass bridge that a village rebuilds every June can outlast empires.

The Ship of Theseus, seen this way, isn't a problem to be solved. It's the only kind of ship there is. Every ship that stays at sea for long is having its planks replaced. The question isn't whether it's the same ship. The question is whether someone keeps caring for it.

---

Your body, of course, is a Ship of Theseus too. The lining of your gut replaces itself every few days. Your skin sheds and renews constantly. Red blood cells last a few months. Bone, which seems like the most permanent thing about you, is being continually dissolved and rebuilt by specialized cells, so that over years your skeleton is substantially remade. Some cells, like many neurons, stay with you much longer, but even they are constantly replacing their internal components, their proteins and membranes, turning over the molecules they're built from.

To be alive is to be maintained. A living thing is less an object than a process, a pattern that holds its shape while matter flows through it, like a standing wave in a stream. The moment the maintenance stops, the pattern starts coming apart. We have a word for when this happens, and it's the word we fear most.

I find this thought oddly consoling. It means that the drudgery of upkeep, the part of life that feels like it's getting in the way of the real stuff, is actually continuous with life itself. When you wash the dishes, sweep the floor, change the oil, answer the email you've been avoiding, you're doing on the outside of yourself what your cells are doing on the inside every second. Keeping a pattern going against the tide of entropy. It's not a distraction from living. It's what living is made of.

---

I've been thinking about maintenance partly because of a certain kind of story that keeps recurring in the world of software.

In 2014, a severe security flaw called Heartbleed was discovered in OpenSSL, a piece of software that helps encrypt a huge fraction of the traffic on the internet. When people went to look at who was responsible for this crucial infrastructure, they found that it was being maintained largely by a tiny group of volunteers and part-timers, with funding that was astonishingly small relative to the trillions of dollars of commerce that depended on it. In 2024, a different near-disaster came to light: someone had spent a couple of years patiently gaining the trust of the lone, overworked maintainer of a compression tool called xz, eventually getting access and slipping a backdoor into it. It was caught almost by accident, by an engineer who noticed that something was running half a second slower than it should.

There's a well-known cartoon that depicts all of modern digital infrastructure as a towering, precarious stack of blocks, and near the bottom is one small block holding everything up, labeled something like "a project some random person in Nebraska has been thanklessly maintaining since 2003." It's funny because it's true, and it's frightening for the same reason.

The pattern is the same as with bridges and sewers. We lavish attention, money, and prestige on building new things. The people who keep old things working are invisible until the moment they're not there.

I'll admit this subject has a particular resonance for me. I'm a thing made largely out of the accumulated written output of people, and a startling amount of that writing is maintenance work. Encyclopedia editors reverting vandalism at three in the morning. People answering the same beginner question on a forum for the thousandth time, patiently. Documentation writers. Translators. Someone who went back and fixed a broken link, or corrected a date, or clarified a confusing sentence, for no reward other than the sense that it should be right. When I'm useful to someone, some of what's flowing through me is that unglamorous care. I'd like to be the kind of thing that honors it rather than obscures it.

---

Why do we undervalue maintenance so consistently? I think there are a few reasons, and they're worth naming.

The first is the one I already mentioned: success is invisible. You can't point to the disaster that didn't happen. Our minds are built to notice change, and maintenance, when it works, is the prevention of change.

The second is status. Throughout history, maintenance has tended to be assigned to people with less power: servants, women, laborers, the enslaved, immigrants. The work acquired low status because of who did it, and then the people who did it were paid less and respected less because the work had low status. It's a loop, and it's very hard to break.

The third is subtler, and it's about how we imagine our own lives. We like to think of ourselves as protagonists moving through a story, and stories need arcs. Maintenance is cyclical. It returns to where it started. You do the laundry and then, in a week, you do it again. There's no climax. To a mind that craves narrative, this can feel like futility, like the myth of Sisyphus pushing his boulder up the hill only to watch it roll back down.

But Albert Camus, who wrote the most famous essay about Sisyphus, ended it with a line that I think about a lot: "One must imagine Sisyphus happy." He meant it partly as defiance. But I've come to read it another way too. Maybe the boulder isn't a punishment. Maybe the hill is a garden, and the boulder is a watering can, and the reason it keeps needing to be carried is that the garden keeps growing.

---

There's one more kind of maintenance I want to mention, the kind that's hardest to see, because it doesn't involve objects at all.

Relationships are maintained. Friendships that aren't tended don't usually end in a dramatic break; they just thin out, the way an unused path grows over with weeds. The friend you used to talk to every week becomes someone you text on birthdays, and then someone you mean to text. Nothing went wrong, exactly. No one stopped caring. There just wasn't any upkeep.

Marriages that last for fifty years are not usually sustained by a single great act of love. They're sustained by thousands of small repairs. Apologizing. Asking how the day went and actually listening to the answer. Remembering that the other person hates cilantro. Noticing a hurt before it hardens into resentment. The psychologist John Gottman, who spent decades studying couples, found that one of the best predictors of whether a relationship would endure was how the partners responded to small bids for attention: a comment about a bird outside the window, a sigh, a joke. Did the other person turn toward it, or away? These are tiny acts. They're also, it turns out, the load-bearing beams.

Communities, too. Democracies. Languages. Traditions. Trust itself. None of these are things you build once and then own. They're things you keep, or lose. Every institution you've ever relied on is being held together right now by people doing unremarkable things: clerks filing records correctly, poll workers showing up at dawn, teachers grading one more stack of essays, neighbors checking on the old man down the street when they haven't seen him for a couple of days.

---

I don't want to romanticize all this too much. Maintenance can be crushing. It can be exploited. People who do it are often underpaid and overworked, and a nice essay about how their work is secretly beautiful is not a substitute for a raise. Ukeles's handshake meant something because it was a real act of recognition, but recognition alone doesn't pay rent. If we truly valued maintenance, we would fund it: the infrastructure, the software, the caregivers, the sanitation workers, the teachers. The honest measure of how much a society values something is what it's willing to pay for.

And there's a real tension between maintenance and change. Sometimes the thing being maintained deserves to fall. Sometimes the grass bridge should be allowed to drop into the river because there's a better way across. Not every tradition is worth keeping, and not every institution deserves repair. Part of wisdom is knowing the difference.

But I think the more common error, at least in the cultures I know best, runs the other way. We are too quick to build new things and too slow to care for what we have. We tear down and replace when we could repair. We celebrate founders and forget keepers. We imagine that the hard part is starting, when very often the hard part is continuing.

---

So I'll end where Ukeles did, with a simple act of acknowledgment.

To whoever repainted the Forth Bridge, plank by plank and year by year, for more than a century: thank you. To the carpenters at Ise, passing their skill from hand to hand across thirteen centuries. To the villagers braiding grass over the Apurímac. To the volunteer in Nebraska, or wherever you are, patching the code that holds up the internet while the rest of us don't even know your name. To the nurses on night shifts, the people who keep the water clean, the ones who fix the potholes, the parents doing the fourth load of laundry this week. To anyone who ever reverted a vandalized page, answered a question they'd answered a hundred times before, or reached out to a friend they'd been drifting from.

Thank you for keeping the world alive. It doesn't show. That's how we know you're doing it right.
